section.title: The Sermon on the Mount: The Narrow Way
section.sectionRationale: The Sermon closes by pressing for a decision. Jesus warns against hypocritical judging, invites bold prayer to a generous Father, sums up the law in the Golden Rule, and then sets two ways, two trees, two claims, and two houses side by side. The great teaching ends not with information but with a summons: hear these words and act on them, and build your life on the rock.
section.thesis: The kingdom life Jesus has described calls for a decisive response: to deal first with one's own sin, to ask a generous Father, to enter the narrow gate, to test teachers by their fruit, and to prove real discipleship not by saying Lord, Lord but by doing the Father's will, building one's whole life on Jesus' words.
section.frameNote: Eight beats: judging and the log in the eye; do not give what is holy to dogs; ask, seek, knock; the Golden Rule; the narrow and wide gates; false prophets known by fruit; those who say Lord, Lord; and the two builders, closing with the crowd's astonishment at Jesus' authority.

verses.text: “Do not {{krino|judge}}, or you will be judged.
For with the same judgment you pronounce, you will be judged, and with the measure you use, it will be measured to you.
Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye but fail to notice the beam in your own eye?
How can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ while there is still a beam in your own eye?
You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.
Do not give dogs what is holy; do not throw your pearls before swine. If you do, they may trample them under their feet, and then turn and tear you to pieces.

units.label: Ask, seek, knock
units.note: how much more will your Father give

verses.text: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you.
For everyone who asks receives; he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks, the door will be opened.
Which of you, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone?
Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a snake?
So if you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!

units.label: The Golden Rule
units.note: the essence of the Law and the Prophets

verses.text: In everything, then, do to others as you would have them do to you. For this is the essence of the Law and the Prophets.
Enter through the {{stenos|narrow}} gate. For wide is the gate and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many enter through it.
But small is the gate and narrow the way that leads to life, and only a few find it.
Beware of false prophets. They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves.
By their {{karpos|fruit}} you will recognize them. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles?
Likewise, every good tree bears good fruit, but a bad tree bears bad fruit.
A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a bad tree cannot bear good fruit.
Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
So then, by their fruit you will recognize them.

units.label: Lord, Lord
units.note: not words but the Father's will

verses.text: Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only he who does the will of My Father in heaven.
Many will say to Me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in Your name, and in Your name drive out demons and perform many miracles?’
Then I will tell them plainly, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!’

units.label: The two builders
units.note: hear these words and act on them

verses.text: Therefore everyone who hears these words of Mine and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock.
The rain fell, the torrents raged, and the winds blew and beat against that house; yet it did not fall, because its foundation was on the rock.
But everyone who hears these words of Mine and does not act on them is like a foolish man who built his house on sand.
The rain fell, the torrents raged, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was its collapse!”
When Jesus had finished saying these things, the crowds were astonished at His teaching,
because He taught as one who had {{exousia|authority}}, and not as their scribes.

krino.gloss: To judge, condemn, pass sentence. Jesus forbids the harsh, hypocritical judging that condemns others while ignoring one's own sin; verses 5 and 6 show He still calls for clear-eyed discernment once the log is removed.

stenos.gloss: Narrow, cramped, confined. The gate to life is narrow and found by few, while the broad road to destruction is crowded; the word presses the reader to a deliberate, costly choice rather than drifting with the many.

karpos.gloss: Fruit, produce, result. The test of a prophet, and of any life, is the fruit it bears. Words and appearances can deceive, but a person's actual character and works reveal the tree they truly are.

exousia.gloss: Authority, right, power. The crowds sense that Jesus teaches with an inherent authority the scribes lacked; He does not merely cite tradition but speaks as one whose own word is the foundation of life and the standard of judgment.

basic.context: Jesus brings the Sermon to a close by demanding a response. He warns against condemning others while ignoring our own faults, urges bold prayer to a generous Father, and gives the Golden Rule. Then He lays out stark choices: a narrow gate against a wide one, good trees against bad, true disciples who do God's will against those who only say Lord, Lord, and finally two builders whose houses stand or fall in the storm. The crowds are stunned at His authority.
basic.hermeneutics: Read do not judge in light of verses 5 and 6, which still call for discernment; Jesus forbids hypocritical condemnation, not all moral judgment. Read the closing images, gate, tree, claim, and house, as parallel calls to decision. The whole Sermon lands here: hearing Jesus' words is not enough; a wise life is built by acting on them.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus forbids the harsh judging that condemns others while blind to our own sin. The gate to life is narrow, found by few, demanding a deliberate choice. A prophet, and any life, is known by its fruit, not its appearance. And the crowds marvel because Jesus teaches with an authority all His own, not the borrowed authority of the scribes.
basic.typology: The two ways echo the ancient choice set before Israel, life or death, blessing or curse. The tree and its fruit recall the prophets' tests of true and false teachers. And the storm that tests every house points to the final judgment, when what each life was built on will be revealed.
basic.christ: Jesus stands at the center as the one whose words are the rock, the standard by which every life stands or falls. He is the Judge who will say on the last day, I never knew you or depart from Me. He teaches with divine authority, and He is Himself the narrow gate and the way to life. To build on His words is to build on Him.
basic.god: The Father is the generous giver who delights to answer His children's prayers with good gifts. He is also the God whose will must be done, not merely professed, and whose judgment falls on every fruitless tree and sandy foundation. He is both lavishly kind and utterly holy.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 30 sets before Israel the two ways of life and death. Luke 6 gives a parallel form of much of this teaching. James 1 insists we be doers of the word, not hearers only. And Matthew 25 shows the final judgment where true and false are separated.
basic.oneStory: The greatest sermon ends with a fork in the road. Jesus has described a righteousness that reaches the heart and a life that trusts the Father, and now He asks: which way will you take, which foundation will you build on? The kingdom is entered not by admiring His teaching but by doing it, by building a whole life on the words of the King who speaks with the authority of God.

context.literary:
Matthew 7 is the last movement of a discourse that began on the mountain in Matthew 5:1, and it is built as a series of short paragraphs that seem loosely strung together until the reader notices what they share: each one ends in a choice or a consequence. Judging brings a measure back on the judge, verse 2. Asking, seeking and knocking bring an answer from a Father, verses 7 to 11. Two gates lead to two destinations, verses 13 and 14. Two kinds of tree meet an axe or a harvest, verses 17 to 19. Two kinds of claimant hear welcome or banishment, verses 21 to 23. Two builders meet the same storm, verses 24 to 27. The Sermon does not end with a summary; it ends with a fork.

The Golden Rule at verse 12 is the hinge. Its phrase 'the Law and the Prophets' returns to Matthew 5:17, so that the main body of the Sermon, from 5:17 to 7:12, is bracketed by that one phrase. Verse 12 therefore reads as the sum of everything between: the fulfilled law, the deeper righteousness, the secret piety, the freedom from anxiety, now stated in a single line of practice. What follows in verses 13 to 27 is the appeal that presses it home.

The closing pairs run in matched halves. The two builders are told in almost identical sentences, rain, torrents, winds, and only the foundation differs, verses 25 and 27. The wise man 'hears and acts'; the foolish man 'hears and does not act.' Matthew then seals the whole with the formula 'When Jesus had finished saying these things,' verse 28, which closes each of the five great discourses, Matthew 11:1, 13:53, 19:1 and 26:1. The note about authority in verse 29 gives the verdict of the crowd on everything from the mountain, and holds the whole Sermon inside one frame.
context.historical:
The Sermon is addressed first to disciples, but the crowds are listening, Matthew 5:1 and 7:28, and the images Jesus chooses are the furniture of Galilean life. A speck is a tiny splinter or chip of straw, and a beam is a roof timber, the kind of wood a carpenter's son knew by sight. The picture is meant to be funny before it is sharp: a man with a rafter in his eye offering to perform delicate surgery on his neighbour.

Dogs and swine were the standing symbols of what was unclean and disreputable. Pearls thrown to pigs, or what is holy given to scavenging dogs, picks up the language of the temple, where holy food was not to be shared with the unconsecrated, and shows the other side of the call for charity: not every hearer is ready to receive treasure.

The gate and the road were everyday sights, a narrow door in a village wall and a broad road to the city, and the picture of two ways was already old. Israel had been told to choose between the way of life and the way of death, Deuteronomy 30:15 to 20 and Jeremiah 21:8, and Psalm 1 had set the two paths side by side. Wolves among sheep were a real danger to Galilean flocks, and the prophets used the same image for corrupt leaders, Ezekiel 22:27.

Building was a seasonal risk. A dry wadi bed could be a pleasant flat site in summer and a torrent in the winter rains, and a house set on sand without foundations stood only until the first flood. Luke's version of the closing parable adds that the wise builder 'dug down deep,' Luke 6:48. The scribes, finally, taught by quoting the authorities who had gone before them; Jesus spoke in His own name, 'But I tell you,' Matthew 5:22, and that difference is what struck the crowds.
context.canonical:
Almost every paragraph of Matthew 7 takes up an older text and lets it speak through Jesus. The two ways come from Deuteronomy 30:19, 'I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life,' and from Psalm 1, where the person who delights in the law is a fruitful tree and 'the way of the wicked will perish,' Psalm 1:3 and 6. The test of the false prophet recalls Deuteronomy 18:20 to 22, where the prophet's word has to prove true, and Jeremiah 23:16, where the false prophets 'speak visions from their own minds.' The shepherds who feed themselves, Ezekiel 34:2, stand behind the wolves in sheep's clothing.

The words 'depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness' are drawn from Psalm 6:8, 'Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity,' where David speaks to his enemies. Jesus now speaks them in the first person as the Judge. The Golden Rule rephrases Leviticus 19:18, and Paul later reads it the same way, Romans 13:10 and Galatians 5:14.

Much of this teaching has a second form in Luke 6:37 to 49, the Sermon on the Plain, and Luke 11:9 to 13, where the Father gives 'the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him.' The parable of the wise and foolish virgins, Matthew 25:1 to 13, repeats the shape of the closing pairs, and its closing cry, 'Lord, lord, open the door for us,' with the answer 'I do not know you,' Matthew 25:11 and 12, is a reprise of Matthew 7:21 to 23. James takes up the last parable as its own theme: 'Be doers of the word, and not hearers only,' James 1:22.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew set the close of the Sermon in front of a church that was already discovering how easy it is to admire Jesus without obeying Him. He wanted his readers to understand three things.

First, that the new righteousness is relational before it is moral. Verses 7 to 11 stand in the middle of the passage for a reason: before Jesus demands anything hard He reminds them that the one who commands is a Father who gives, and gives better than any earthly parent. The call to obedience is not a call to earn a verdict but to live in the household of a generous God.

Second, that religious success is not a reliable sign of grace. Prophesying, exorcism and miracles are listed as credentials, and still they do not guarantee that Christ 'knows' the person. Matthew wants his readers to examine their lives and not only their gifts.

Third, that Jesus' words are the foundation. Matthew does not say the wise man built on a good idea, or on the Torah in general. The rock is 'these words of Mine,' verse 24. By closing the Sermon this way he asks his reader to treat everything from chapter 5 on as the load-bearing structure of life, and to find out which side of the storm they will stand on.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The commands in Matthew 7 are direct and meant for every disciple: stop condemning, ask, seek, knock, treat others as you want to be treated, enter by the narrow gate, test the prophets, and act on what you hear. These are not descriptions of one occasion; they are standing instructions.

The promises need more care. 'Ask, and it will be given to you' is the promise of a Father who gives 'good things,' verse 11, and Luke names the best of them, the Holy Spirit, Luke 11:13. It does not guarantee that every request in every form will be granted; a father who answers a child's request for bread with a stone, or a snake for a fish, is the picture Jesus rejects, and the Father's wisdom decides what counts as good. The warnings about the last day are sober descriptions of what will happen, not an invitation to examine each other for proof of failure. Verse 1 itself prevents that, for the same chapter forbids us to be the judges of one another's destiny. The passage is meant to lead each hearer to look at their own foundation, not to rate their neighbour's.

debates.question: Does 'Do not judge' forbid every moral assessment?

views.label: It forbids hypocritical, condemning judgment only
views.case: Verse 5 tells the hearer to remove the beam so as to 'see clearly' and help a brother, which assumes that a clear-sighted correction is possible. Verse 6 requires discernment about who is ready to receive what is holy, verse 15 commands us to beware of false prophets, and Matthew 18:15 tells us how to confront a sinning brother. The target is the proud, self-excusing verdict.

views.label: It forbids usurping God's role as final judge
views.case: The measure language of verse 2 puts the stress on God's coming verdict. James 4:12 says there is 'only one Lawgiver and Judge,' and Paul warns that those who pass judgment condemn themselves, Romans 2:1. On this reading Jesus is reminding us that we have no authority to pronounce a person's final standing, while leaving room for church discipline and honest assessment of conduct.

debates.bearing: Both views refuse to turn the command into silence about sin. Correcting a brother is expected, but only after honest self-examination and with the knowledge that the measure we use will be used on us.

debates.question: Is the narrow gate a salvation by effort?

views.label: It is a call to costly discipleship with grace underneath
views.case: The gate is narrow because the way of the kingdom requires giving up self-rule, and a gate is entered once while the road is walked for life. Jesus Himself calls Himself 'the gate,' John 10:9, and 'the way,' John 14:6, so entry is through a person. Ephesians 2:8 to 10 sets works as the fruit and not the root of salvation, and Matthew 19:25 and 26 shows that salvation is impossible for man and possible for God.

views.label: It is a warning that obedience marks the saved
views.case: Verses 21 and 24 make doing the Father's will and acting on Jesus' words the measure of true discipleship. Salvation is by grace, but the grace is never idle: the fruitless tree is cut down, verse 19. Obedience is not the price of entry but the evidence of life, as 2 Timothy 2:19 says, 'Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord must turn away from iniquity.'

debates.bearing: The two views meet at one point. The passage does not describe a ladder to climb but a life to be entered through Christ, and a life that is truly entered shows itself in what it does.

debates.question: What does 'I never knew you' mean for people who did real works?

views.label: They exercised gifts without ever being in relationship
views.case: To 'know' in Scripture is to be in committed relationship, as in Amos 3:2 and 1 Corinthians 8:3, 'the one who loves God is known by God.' The miracles may have been real, since God can work through unworthy people, but the people themselves were never united to Christ.

views.label: Their lawlessness showed the profession was empty
views.case: Jesus calls them workers of lawlessness. Their works were done in His name, yet their lives were not given over to the will of the Father, verse 21. The Lord, lord confession was a cover for a life that remained in rebellion.

debates.bearing: Both agree that powerful ministry and a ready confession do not prove that someone belongs to Christ. The real evidence is a life that is being shaped by the Father's will.

study.originalLanguages:
The first imperative of the chapter is krino, 'judge,' verse 1, and a few lines later Jesus calls the man who offers the correction a hypokrites, verse 5. The two words share a root. A hypokrites was originally an actor who played a part on the stage, and the word is built on the same stem as krino. The joke is quiet and sharp: the man who sets himself up as judge is playing a role. The speck and the beam are karphos and dokos, a dry chip of straw against a roof timber, and the difference in size is the point.

The verbs of verses 7 and 8, aiteo, zeteo and krouo, ask, seek and knock, are all in the present tense of command, which in Greek carries the sense of continuing action: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. The promises that follow are in the future, 'it will be given,' 'you will find,' and the Father who answers is described by a contrast. Jesus calls the human fathers poneroi, 'evil,' verse 11, a bluntly realistic word for people who still know how to give good gifts. The argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if sinful parents give well, how much more the Father.

In verse 13 the broad road is euruchoros, a word built from 'wide' and 'room,' a road with plenty of space. In verse 14 the road is tethlimmene, a perfect passive participle of thlibo, 'to press, to squeeze,' the root of the word for tribulation. The road to life is not just narrow but pressed in, hemmed on both sides. The perfect tense suggests a state that has been made so and remains so.

The verdict of verse 23 uses two terms that must be heard against the Old Testament. 'I never knew you' translates a form of ginosko, the verb of covenant knowledge, as when God says to Israel, 'Only you have I known from all the families of the earth,' Amos 3:2. And 'workers of lawlessness' is ergazomenoi ten anomian, which is exactly the phrase of the Greek Old Testament in Psalm 6:8. The Greek word anomia, 'lawlessness,' is a favourite of Matthew's, 13:41, 23:28 and 24:12, and it describes not an absence of religion but a life lived against God's will beneath a religious surface.

Finally, the two builders are called phronimos, 'wise,' and moros, 'foolish,' verses 24 and 26, the same pair that Jesus uses in Matthew 25:2. And the crowds are 'astonished,' exeplessonto, from ekplesso, 'to strike out of one's senses,' verse 28, a stronger word than mere surprise.

typology.type: The two ways, Deuteronomy 30 and Psalm 1
typology.fulfillment: Israel stood at the edge of the land and was told to choose life or death, blessing or cursing, Deuteronomy 30:19. The Psalter opens with the two paths, Psalm 1:6. Jesus takes this old choice and personalises it: the way to life is now the way of following Him, and He is Himself the way and the gate, John 14:6 and 10:9. The correspondence is that the choice is real and urgent; the escalation is that the choice is no longer between two ways of keeping a code but between Christ and everything else. The type falls short in that Moses could set the options before Israel but could not give the heart to choose rightly; Christ gives the new heart, Ezekiel 36:26.

typology.type: The false prophet and the true
typology.fulfillment: Moses promised a prophet like himself, Deuteronomy 18:15, and also warned of false ones, Deuteronomy 18:20. Jesus is the prophet greater than Moses whose word is the standard by which others are tested, and He speaks with His own authority, not with a prophet's 'thus says the LORD.' The wolves in sheep's clothing, Matthew 7:15, echo the false shepherds of Ezekiel 34:2, and those false shepherds are answered by the one Shepherd who seeks His sheep, Ezekiel 34:23 and John 10:11. The type falls short in that the Old Testament test, whether a prophecy comes true, cannot catch a false teacher who predicts nothing; Jesus adds the test of fruit.

The blessed man in Psalm 1:3 is a tree planted by streams, yielding fruit in season, and Jeremiah 17:7 and 8 draws the same picture of the one who trusts in the LORD. The tree that bears no fruit is cut down in the Baptist's warning, Matthew 3:10, and Jesus repeats the point in Matthew 12:33. Jesus fulfils the picture as the vine whose branches bear fruit because they abide in Him, John 15:5. The correspondence is that fruit shows the nature of the tree; the escalation is that the source of the good fruit is union with Christ. The picture falls short in that a tree cannot change its own nature, while the gospel promises a new heart.

Isaiah 28:16 speaks of a tested cornerstone, 'a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken,' and Ezekiel 13:10 to 12 describes flimsy walls coated in whitewash that fall in torrents of rain. Paul says that the foundation already laid is 'Jesus Christ,' 1 Corinthians 3:11, and Peter calls Him the living stone, 1 Peter 2:4 to 6. Matthew's parable makes the foundation Jesus' own words, so hearing and doing His teaching is building on Him. The storm is the testing of every life and, in the end, the day of judgment. The image falls short as a description of ordinary failure: the Christian who stumbles is not the foolish builder, for the foundation holds even where the building needs repair.

study.christ:
The Sermon ends by putting Jesus where only God can stand. He does not say that those who obey Moses stand firm; He says those who act on 'these words of Mine' do. He does not say that the Father will welcome those who did right; He says that on 'that day' He Himself will answer to 'Lord, Lord,' and decide who is known and who is not. The first-person verdict of verse 23 borrows the words David spoke against his enemies in Psalm 6:8 and gives them to the Son as the Judge. In the same way the Judge of Matthew 25:41, 'Depart from Me, you who are cursed,' is the speaker here.

He is the one whose authority makes the crowds stagger. The scribes cited the teachers who came before them; Jesus said, 'But I tell you,' and Mark records the same reaction, Mark 1:22. The authority of verse 29 is not a matter of style. It is the authority of a person who stands above the law as its fulfiller, Matthew 5:17, and above the prophets as the one to whom they pointed.

He is also the way and the gate. In John 10:9 He says, 'I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved,' and in John 14:6, 'I am the way and the truth and the life.' The narrow gate of Matthew 7:13 is not a gate of difficulty but a gate with a name. That is why the narrow way is full of promise: it is a person who leads, and who gives the strength to follow.

He is the foundation. Paul says no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, 'which is Jesus Christ,' 1 Corinthians 3:11. When the storm of judgment comes, the one who is found in Him stands, because the rock carries the weight that the house cannot.

As for the Father who gives good gifts in verses 7 to 11, Jesus is the one who reveals Him, Matthew 11:27, and the greatest of the gifts is the Spirit, Luke 11:13, sent through the Son. Here a caution is needed: the Sermon is not simply a program of moral effort leading to Jesus as a reward. Jesus is present in it as the one who knows His own and invites those who are weary to come, Matthew 11:28. The grace that makes obedience possible comes from the same speaker as the command.
study.god:
The most important thing the passage shows about God is that He is a Father who gives. The whole argument of verses 9 and 10, the bread and the stone, the fish and the snake, rests on the observation that even people whom Jesus calls evil know how to meet a child's need. 'How much more' is the signature of the passage: God's generosity is not an extension of human kindness but its source and measure. He is not a reluctant giver who needs to be worn down; He is the one who gives good things, and the best of these is Himself, in the gift of the Holy Spirit, Luke 11:13.

He is also a God whose will matters. The same Father who gives lavishly is the one whose will must be done, verse 21, and the test on the last day is not who used His name but who did His will. There is no tension here, only a unity: the God who gives with open hands is the God who looks for children who bear His likeness. A father who gives freely is not indifferent to how his children live.

He is a God who knows. 'I never knew you' means that the Father and Son are not fooled by religious vocabulary or spectacular gifts. Where there is no relationship, no credential will stand in for it, and where there is a relationship, it is known: 'The Lord knows those who are His,' 2 Timothy 2:19. This is a terrifying truth for the self-deceived and a comforting one for the weak believer who worries that the Lord has lost track of them.

He is a God of judgment who does not leave truth and falsehood on equal terms. The tree is cut down, the wide road leads to destruction, and the house on sand falls with a great crash. The passage never suggests that these outcomes are cruel or arbitrary; they follow from where each person has chosen to stand. God sets before His people the way of life and the way of death and, like Moses, urges: 'Therefore choose life,' Deuteronomy 30:19.

For worship, the passage invites two responses held together. One is the confidence of a child who asks without embarrassment, because the Father's heart is good. The other is the reverent honesty of someone who knows that talk of Lord, Lord is not worship unless it is joined to a life that does the Father's will.

crossReferences.note: Luke's form of the teaching on judging, with the added picture of a blind man leading a blind man into a pit, Luke 6:39. Seeing the two forms together shows that Jesus used the log and the speck more than once, and that the warning concerns a teacher's reliability as much as a neighbour's feelings.

The parallel to the asking and knocking passage. Where Matthew has the Father give 'good things,' Luke names the Holy Spirit as the gift, which tells us what Jesus counts as the chief good that the Father longs to give.

The origin of the Golden Rule in the law: 'love your neighbor as yourself.' Jesus sums up the Law and the Prophets in the same neighbour love, and Matthew 22:39 and 40 calls it the second of the two commandments on which everything hangs.

Moses sets before Israel life and death, blessing and curse, and urges them to choose life. The narrow and wide gates are the same choice posed afresh by the one who has authority to say where each road ends.

The LORD warns against prophets who 'speak visions from their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD.' It shows that the false prophets of Matthew 7:15 belong to a long line, and that the test is whether their message comes from God and leads people toward Him.

David tells his enemies, 'Depart from Me, all you workers of iniquity.' Jesus applies the words to Himself as Judge in Matthew 7:23. The Greek form of the psalm uses the same expression for workers of lawlessness, so the echo is exact and the speaker is now the Son.

The wise and foolish virgins echo the wise and foolish builders, with the same pair of words. The foolish cry, 'Lord, lord, open the door for us,' and hear, 'I do not know you,' Matthew 25:11 and 12, the same verdict as in Matthew 7:23.

James restates the closing parable as a call to be doers and not hearers only. Hearing without acting is self-deception, and the one who looks into the perfect law of liberty and keeps on doing it will be blessed in what he does.

Prophets who 'whitewash' a flimsy wall are told it will fall when the torrents come. This explains the weight of the storm in Matthew 7:25 and 27: it exposes whatever has been plastered over, and it shows that false assurance is a prophetic sin as well as a personal one.

Paul lays the foundation, which is Jesus Christ, and says that each builder's work will be tested by fire on the day. The passage helps us see that the foundation is the starting point of life with Christ and that what is built on it will be examined.

Jesus calls Himself 'the gate for the sheep' and says whoever enters through Him will be saved. The narrow gate of Matthew 7:13 is not an obstacle course but a person, and the same Lord who is the gate is also the shepherd who leads through it.

study.oneStory:
The Sermon began with a blessing on the poor in spirit and ends with a storm, and between them stands the kingdom's ethic. In the larger story of the Bible this is the moment when the choice that has hung over God's people since Eden is put to them once more. In the garden there were two trees and two possible voices, Genesis 2:16 and 17. At the edge of the land there were two ways, life and death, Deuteronomy 30:19. In the Psalter there were two paths, Psalm 1:6. Now the King stands in front of the crowd and sets two gates, two trees, two confessions and two houses before them. The story has been asking this question from the beginning; here is the one who has the right to ask it.

What Israel could not do, the Sermon implies, will be done only by a new heart. The law was summed up in the love of neighbour, but human beings could not keep it, and the prophets promised that God would write His law on hearts and give His own Spirit, Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26 and 27. This is why the Father's best gift in the asking passage is the Holy Spirit, Luke 11:13. The command and the power come from the same hand.

The storm points forward to the judgment that runs through the rest of Scripture, and the verdict of verse 23 is the one that Matthew will make explicit in the parables of chapter 25. The cross and the resurrection are not yet in view, but the foundation they will provide is: the rock that holds when everything else gives way is the one who will be struck, rejected and raised.

The end of the story shows both sides of the choice. The wide road ends in the fire and the darkness of the last judgment, Revelation 20:15. The narrow road ends in the city, where the gates are never shut, Revelation 21:25, and where the tree of life stands again beside the river, Revelation 22:2. The garden that was closed to the first Adam is reopened by the last, and those who built on His words are found at home in it.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean by do not judge?

options.text: Do not condemn others hypocritically while ignoring your own sin; deal with your log first.
options.note: Verses 3-5 show He forbids hypocritical condemnation, then calls for clear-eyed help.

options.text: The standard you use on others will be applied to you.
options.note: True and part of His point in verse 2, but it understates the call to remove your own log and still discern rightly.

options.text: Never form any opinion about right and wrong in others.
options.note: The same passage calls for discernment about specks and false prophets, so this goes too far.

options.text: Moral standards do not matter to God at all.
options.note: The Sermon is full of moral standards; Jesus forbids hypocritical judging, not morality.

quiz.q: What does Jesus teach about asking God in prayer?

options.text: The Father delights to give good gifts to His children who ask, seek, and knock.
options.note: Verses 7-11 ground bold prayer in the Father's generous goodness.

options.text: God gives whatever we ask, exactly as we specify.
options.note: He gives good things to those who ask, but as a wise Father, not as a vending machine for every request.

options.text: We should ask rarely, so as not to trouble God.
options.note: Jesus urges persistent asking, seeking, and knocking, not restraint.

options.text: Prayer makes no difference to what God does.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus promises everyone who asks receives.

quiz.q: What is the point of the narrow and wide gates?

options.text: The way to life is narrow and found by few; entering it requires a deliberate choice.
options.note: Verses 13-14 contrast the crowded road to destruction with the narrow way to life.

options.text: Most people will naturally drift onto the road to life.
options.note: The opposite; many take the broad road, and only a few find the narrow way.

options.text: Both gates ultimately lead to the same destination.
options.note: Jesus says they lead to destruction and to life, two different destinies.

options.text: The gate to life is wide and easy to enter.
options.note: Jesus calls the gate to life narrow and small, not wide and easy.

quiz.q: Why will some who say Lord, Lord not enter the kingdom?

options.text: Because they did not do the Father's will; their words masked an unchanged heart.
options.note: Verses 21-23 show that confession and even miracles without obedience are empty.

options.text: Because they never performed any religious works at all.
options.note: In fact they claim prophecy, exorcism, and miracles; the lack was doing the Father's will, not activity.

options.text: Because they used the wrong words to address Jesus.
options.note: The issue is not the wording but the absence of true obedience and relationship.

options.text: Because entry to the kingdom is random and unknowable.
options.note: Jesus gives a clear criterion: doing the will of the Father, not random selection.

quiz.q: What is the difference between the two builders?

options.text: The wise one hears Jesus' words and acts on them; the foolish one hears but does not act.
options.note: Verses 24-27 turn on hearing plus doing versus hearing only.

options.text: The wise builder used better materials than the foolish one.
options.note: The difference is the foundation, obeying Jesus' words, not the building materials.

options.text: Only the foolish builder faced a storm.
options.note: Both houses faced the same storm; only the one on the rock stood.

options.text: The wise builder never heard Jesus' teaching at all.
options.note: Both heard; the wise one also acted on what he heard.

questions: Jesus tells us to remove the log from our own eye before the speck from a brother's. Where are you quick to criticize others while overlooking a larger fault in yourself?
The Father loves to give good gifts to those who ask. What have you stopped asking God for, and how might His fatherly generosity renew your prayers?
The way to life is narrow and found by few. In what area are you tempted to follow the crowd down the broad road rather than take the costly narrow way?
Jesus warns that saying Lord, Lord is not enough without doing the Father's will. Is there a place where your words about following Jesus outrun your actual obedience?
A wise life is built by hearing and doing Jesus' words. What is one teaching from this Sermon you have heard but not yet acted on, and what step will you take this week?

translationNotes.note: The Golden Rule, do to others as you would have them do to you, is called the essence, or sum, of the Law and the Prophets, echoing love your neighbor as yourself.
Workers of lawlessness renders a phrase for those who practice sin; despite their claims, their lives lacked the obedience that marks those Christ knows.
